content.summary_of_the_paper:
Authors proposed a novel explainable deep learning model (AxBERT) for Chinese spelling correction by aligning with an associative knowledge network (AKN). 

In the empirical study, results on SIGHAN datasets demonstrate that AxBERT can achieve extraordinary performance, especially upon model precision compared to baselines. Also authors claim the explainability of AxBERT is better than the baseline.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
Authors proposed an interesting novel method which improve the performance of spell correction in Chinese. Authors shows it achieves better performance compared to multiple recent benchmarks.

Weaknesses
The impact of this project is my major concern. It would be more impact if authors can generalize such methodology to other similar languages and shows the generalization of the methodology. If it only improves Chinese, I think it may fit to some NLP conference, instead of general conference like ICLR as it may not be significant to the most of the audience. In addition, the application is only applied to spelling correction on one dataset, thus it lack of evidence how such innovation can be generalize to other application/task/dataset.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity

The experiment part is clear and I appreciate authors' effort in comparing the proposed method with a wide range of recent propose benchmarks. However, I am concerned the 'model explainability' section is a bit weak. I am not very convinced by the case in the section on how the new model can be explained better and easier.

Quality and Novelty

As the dataset used in the experiment is Chinese and thus less well known for the whole community, it would be helpful to add more details in the performance comparison to help readers to understand how significant is the improvement. I would recommend authors run the experiment multiple times and report standard error/confidence interval for the metrics.


Reproducibility
I was not able to find the code link. Given the data is public available, I think it would be reproducible if authors can open-source the experiment script.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I think it is an interesting paper, with thorough experiment and exciting performance improvement. However, given the limitation (the methodology only apply to one task for one language and only analyzed on a certain dataset) I am afraid it may not be a good fit for a general conference like ICLR. If author can add more insight and potential extension of this work for broader audience, I am glad to reconsider my evaluation.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes an method  dubbed "AxBERT" to deal with  Chinese spelling correction. 
AxBERT uses an Associative knowledge network. Essentially, it follows that characters co-occurred in phrases are considered associated, and an associative knowledge network is employed to model this language logic information.
The authors further provide the model design. To align the uninterpretable BERT logic with the interpretable statistical logic, the authors designed an alignment task to reduce this gap, and adopted the multi-task learning paradigm to train the alignment task and the correction task in parallel.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strength 
- Chinese spelling correction is an interesting task and it seems the method work well.
- 

## Weaknesses
- More experimental details should be introduced 
- Explainability was highlighted in the introduction, but the explainability in this paper is not that convincing.
- It focuses only Chinese spelling correction, which seems narrow for ICLR community. If the method is not specific to Chinese, consider benchmarking it in English dataset, otherwise it is fine.
- It seems AxBERT is comparable to PLOME, the authors might need to find a better way to evidence the significance of the method.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is fairly well written

## Question 

- There are no details about the raw BERT implemenation [Devlin et al., 2019]. It seems in the paper that performance of raw BERT  is much better than  HeadFilt and PLOME. But in their paper (HeadFilt and PLOME),  the perfromance of BERT is much worse than  HeadFilt /PLOME. Do the authors use a better-trained BERT backbone?

- Why do the authors set the \lambad as 0.8 (from formula 14)?

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces an explainable model called AxBERT, which uses driven by semantic alignment and regulation. Transformer-based models show good results in spelling correction but has the problem of being unable to explain. To tackle the above questions, the paper proposes associative knowledge network (AKN) and a weight regulator. AKN is used to build the relationships between Chinese characters, and the weight regulator is built to adjust the attention distributions in BERT to reduce the influence of irrelevant characters. Experiment results show that AxBERT achieve great performance and has good explainability.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The idea that introducing associative knowledge network to enhance the explainability of the CSC model is evolutionary. The model still achieves good performance with explainability.
2. The paper notices the layer-wise analysis results and prevents different layer functions from making the model hard to explain.
3. The section of case study uses various colors and diagrams to show the contrast between original model and proposed model.

Weaknesses:
1. The associative matrix is based on AKN, which is illustrated in formula 1, but the distance the paper uses is not explained clearly. Is it the simple character distance or the embedding distance?
2. The use of weight regulator can make the model focus more on the relevant characters, but the results show that the model doesn’t show good results on character-level than the sentence-level. It may be caused by lacking information of the original character. Maybe further ablation study can be done to explain the reason.
3. Table 2 simply changes the color of the word, but doesn’t show the difference after regulation, is it a mistake?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Some crucial technical descriptions need to be further clarified. The technical contribution and novelty are also limited.
content.summary_of_the_review: Research about model explainability is encouraged. However, some crucial technical descriptions need to be further clarified, and the technical contribution and novelty are also limited. Therefore, this paper need to be further improved to touch the bar of the conference.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a novel explainable BERT-based Chinese spelling correction model by aligning with an associative knowledge network. The paper uses a least-squares function to quantify the BERT layer. The paper also uses a translator matrix to map statistical and BERT logic. The paper then introduces a character-level similarity between attention and associative knowledge network to regulate attention distribution, The paper is tested on three different datasets and achieves comparable results. The paper also provides a case study.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The paper proposes a new method to correct Chinese spelling in an explainable way. The authors compare the proposed methods with multiple state-of-the-art baselines. The case study shows that the proposed method is useful.


Weaknesses:
1. Some parts of the paper are not clearly written, which will be discussed in the clarity section. 

2. The paper claims that it has evaluated with SIGHAN, HybirdSet, and CLUE. However, I only see the results of SIGHAN. The rest two datasets are not included in the paper. The proposed methods also fail to outperform other baselines significantly. It might be helpful to have those two extra datasets in the results. The analysis in section 4.5 is too superficial. The authors need to include a more insightful analysis by qualitatively comparing the results of the proposed methods with baselines. Authors fail to include any ablation study for the proposed method.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1. Some details of the paper is not clear. Some figures are hard to follow. For example, Figure 1 tries to show the information flow. However, from the introduction, the motivation behind the transforming matrix and associative matrix is unclear. It would be better to represent the symbols listed in the caption of Figure 3 in the actual figure. Currently, it is hard for readers to catch those ideas. Figure 6 needs to include tokens for all three attention maps (Subfigure a b c).  Readers have a hard time mapping the token pairs with corresponding matrix weights.  Equation 2 seems to be incorrect. The denominator should be $Avg(A_i)$ instead of $Avg(M_{S_i})$. Section 4.6 is weird. More background needs to be given for this analysis. Which dataset is used for this explainable analysis? 

2. The paper provides some implementation details. However, the paper doesn't provide any code or training details for reproduction.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper proposes an interesting explainable spelling correction model. However, many parts of the paper are hard to understand. I think the paper needs to be revised for better understanding.
